The United States has a strong national defense that depends on multiple factors including a robust economy and diverse fuel banks.
This year’s NDAA supports U.S. warfighters’ readiness across all spectrums of conflict.
China, Russia, and Iran are investing heavily in advanced military technologies.
Elected officials have a responsibility to support those who protect the nation.
The NDAA aligns with the President's 2018 National Defense Strategy, the first new strategy in ten years.
Consumer choice in energy is considered a positive outcome by the speaker.
The speaker co-led efforts with Senator Martin Heinrich to increase funding for innovative technologies in hypersonics, unmanned systems, directed energy, and artificial intelligence.
Renewable fuels are a significant part of America’s energy strategy and contribute to economic growth and job creation.

The effectiveness of U.S. military strength relies on continuous investment in innovation and modernization.
The speaker believes that the current administration’s approach to defense policy is superior to past administrations, especially the Obama era.
General James Mattis is a competent and effective leader whose strategic vision enhances national defense.
President Trump’s support for the military and veterans strengthens national unity and deterrence capability.
Energy resilience through diversified fuel sources—including renewables—is a core component of national security.
Adversaries like Russia, China, and Iran represent credible and escalating threats to U.S. interests.
The Renewable Fuel Standard (RFS) is a successful public policy instrument that advances national interests.
Congressional action, particularly through bipartisan legislation, is necessary to rebuild military capacity after previous cuts.
Maintaining or regaining a technological edge requires sustained political commitment and funding prioritization.

Rural America is the backbone of our country, and the RFS is an invaluable economic engine, creating good paid jobs, raising incomes, increasing tax revenues, and offering new investment opportunities. My home state of Iowa leads the nation in renewable fuels production with 43 ethanol refineries capable of producing 4 billion gallons annually and 12 biodiesel facilities producing over 350 million gallons annually. In 2017, the renewable fuels industry created $2.4 billion in household income and supported nearly 50,000 jobs in my home state of Iowa. Such jobs and investment are critical in rural areas. It's what we need to find long-term and sustainable success for struggling communities. The success we see in Iowa represents only a fraction of the economic impact seen across the 28 states with an ethanol facility. Last year, our nation's ethanol industry supported more than 350,000 American jobs and increased U.S. household income by $24 billion. Just one example, in Atlantic Iowa, a new ethanol plant is ramping up production. In Atlantic, it was just a little bit further north of where I live, next county up. Once the plant reaches full capacity, the $196 million project will support 49 full-time jobs and not only be a boon for Cass County, but also corn farmers in surrounding counties like my home county of Montgomery County. There are countless examples like this all across the Midwest. This investment rural development is a direct result of the success of the certainty provided by the RFS. The economic effects are increasingly widespread. And this all underscores the importance of a strong RFS today and well into the future. Now, over the past several months, I have stressed to President Trump and our Senate colleagues during multiple White House meetings that many across the Midwest, they already know this, that a strong and robust RFS encourages consumer choice, investment, and innovation. And it protects the diverse fuel mix which helps keep our nation more secure. Small-town livelihoods like Charlie Goodes, owner of Good and Quick in Nevada, Iowa, take it from Charlie, someone who has spent 20 years, he installed blender pumps and transitioned to flex fuels, which are E15 and higher blends. E15 is a term for higher octane fuel that is currently available in 28 states at retail fueling stations. It's 15% ethanol and 85% gasoline and is approved for the use in more than 80% of our cars, trucks, and SUVs on the road today. Retailers offer E-15 for many reasons, but it often has a lower cost than regular unleaded fuel. Earlier this month, farmers breathed a sigh of relief and applauded when the president rejected the idea of overhauling and fundamentally changing the current biofuels policy in a way that is less accountable to the American people. We are a nation of laws and the federal government must uphold them in an accountable way. Moving forward, I will continue working tirelessly alongside our corn state colleagues to protect and defend the RFS. which is working for corn farmers, ethanol producers, retailers, and our rural communities. Difficult times have fallen on rural America, especially on our farmers, and any attempt to undermine the RFS will only make matters worse. But our agricultural community and renewable fuels industry know that I stand ready to defend, protect, and grow a strong, robust RFS that encourages consumer choice, investment, and innovation. And again, thanks for having me here today. I would love to take as many questions as possible. So thank you all very much. I appreciate it.

explicit_propositions.text: The Renewable Fuel Standard (RFS) is vital to the people of Iowa and rural America.
Rural America is the backbone of the United States.
The RFS serves as an invaluable economic engine in rural areas.
The RFS creates good-paying jobs, raises incomes, increases tax revenues, and offers new investment opportunities.
Iowa leads the nation in renewable fuels production with 43 ethanol refineries and 12 biodiesel facilities.
These refineries produce 4 billion gallons of ethanol annually and 350 million gallons of biodiesel annually.
In 2017, the renewable fuels industry generated $2.4 billion in household income and supported nearly 50,000 jobs in Iowa.
Jobs and investments driven by the RFS are essential for long-term sustainability in rural communities.
The economic impact of the RFS extends beyond Iowa to 28 other states with ethanol facilities.
Last year, the national ethanol industry supported over 350,000 American jobs and increased U.S. household income by $24 billion.

assumptions.text: The speaker believes that maintaining legal consistency in federal policy fosters trust and predictability for investors and businesses.
The speaker assumes that economic prosperity in rural areas depends heavily on sustained government mandates like the RFS.
The speaker holds that supporting renewable fuels aligns with national energy security and independence.
The speaker trusts personal anecdotes and local business owners (like Charlie Goodes) as credible evidence of broader systemic benefits.
The speaker assumes that opposing changes to the RFS reflects loyalty to both farmers and small-town values.
The speaker believes that political leadership should prioritize rural economic interests over urban or environmental concerns.
The speaker views the RFS as a mechanism that enables technological adoption (e.g., E15) and infrastructure upgrades (e.g., blender pumps).
The speaker assumes that public support for the RFS is broad among Midwestern constituents and farmers.
The speaker sees federal law enforcement and accountability as central to democratic legitimacy and effective governance.
The speaker believes that undermining the RFS would disproportionately harm vulnerable rural populations and their economies.
